source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris

facts.text: 100% of the population in Greece is eligible for a core set of health services (OECD average 98%, 2024).
Only 27% of people in Greece were satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 64%; satisfaction in Greece has deteriorated over time.
Greece had the lowest satisfaction with the availability of quality health services among OECD countries; fewer than 50% were satisfied in Greece, Türkiye, Hungary, Italy, Chile and Colombia.

Only 60.9% of health spending in Greece was covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 75.1% — so 39.1% was not covered by public or compulsory schemes (OECD 24.9%).
Households in Greece had to bear more than one-third of all healthcare costs directly out of pocket (OECD average: just under one-fifth).

Public and compulsory schemes covered only 63% of hospital care costs in Greece in 2023, versus 89% on average in the OECD; in Greece and Korea public coverage of inpatient care was only around two-thirds.
Public and compulsory schemes covered 62% of outpatient medical care costs in Greece in 2023, versus 78% on average in the OECD.
Public and compulsory schemes covered 0% of dental care costs in Greece in 2023, versus 32% on average in the OECD.
Public and compulsory schemes covered 52% of pharmaceutical costs in Greece in 2023, versus 58% on average in the OECD.
Inpatient care made up 34% of out-of-pocket spending in Greece, versus 8% across OECD countries, reflecting outlays for privately provided hospital services.
12.1% of people in Greece reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 — the highest among 28 OECD countries with comparable data (OECD average 3.4%).
Cost was the main reason for unmet medical care needs in Greece.
In Greece more than one in six people in the lowest income group reported unmet medical care needs; the income gap in unmet needs was among the largest in the OECD.
Unmet medical care needs due to waiting times have increased in Greece since 2019; Greece launched the Unified Digital List of Surgeries in 2024 to centralise state hospital surgery waiting lists.
More than 8% of people in Greece reported unmet dental care needs in 2024, versus fewer than 1% in Germany and the Netherlands.
In Greece 15% of people living in cities and 43% in rural areas lived far from a hospital; Greece had the highest share of unmet needs due to distance to travel among 28 OECD countries.
57% of patients with chronic conditions in Greece trusted the last healthcare professional they saw — the lowest among participating OECD countries (OECD average 78%).

Over 50% of primary care users aged 45 and over in Greece reported an event that could have caused them unnecessary harm, such as not getting an appointment when needed or a delayed diagnosis — among the highest rates.
